visuals.title: Where haemorrhoids sit
visuals.text: Anal cushions at the end of the bowel; the liver matters because portal hypertension worsens them.

glossary.Anal canal: The last 3 to 4 cm of the gut, running from the rectum to the anus.
glossary.Arteriovenous: Linking arteries directly to veins, as in the blood-filled anal cushions.
glossary.Anaemia: Low haemoglobin, here from slow, repeated blood loss.
glossary.Ulceration: Breakdown of the surface lining to form an open sore.
glossary.Columnar: Tall, column-shaped lining cells typical of the gut above the dentate line.
glossary.Transitional mucosa: A zone of lining where gut-type cells change to skin-type cells.
glossary.Squamous epithelium: Flat, layered skin-type lining, here below the dentate line.
glossary.Insensate: Unable to feel pain or touch.
glossary.Somatically innervated: Supplied by somatic nerves, which sense sharp, well-localised pain.
glossary.Haemorrhoidal plexus: The network of veins in the anal cushions.
glossary.Stool softeners: Laxatives such as docusate that make stool softer and easier to pass.
glossary.Bulk-forming laxative: Fibre that holds water in the stool, making it bulkier and softer.
glossary.Emollient: A soothing cream or ointment that softens and protects the skin.
glossary.Topical: Applied directly to the skin or surface.
glossary.Local anaesthetic: A drug, such as lidocaine, that numbs a small area.
glossary.Contraindicated: Should not be used because it may cause harm.
glossary.Infra-red photocoagulation: Infra-red light used to scar and shrink small internal haemorrhoids.
glossary.Oesophageal varices: Dilated veins in the lower oesophagus caused by portal hypertension; they can bleed heavily.
glossary.Fibrosis: Scar tissue formation that fixes tissue in place.
glossary.Slough: To die and fall away from living tissue.
glossary.Intra-abdominal pressure: Pressure inside the abdomen, raised by straining, pregnancy and obesity.
glossary.Anal margin: The edge where the anal canal meets the skin.
glossary.Red flags: Features suggesting serious disease, such as weight loss or change in bowel habit, that need further tests.
glossary.Adjunct: A treatment added to the main treatment.
glossary.Systemic symptoms: Whole-body symptoms such as fever and weight loss.
glossary.Pregnancy: Raises pelvic venous pressure and causes constipation, so haemorrhoids are common.
